newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Rouble still seen safe from speculative attack.
newsitem.headline: Rouble still seen safe from speculative attack.

text.p: The rouble, tightly controlled by the Russian central bank, is virtually immune from the sort of international speculative attack suffered recently by the Thai baht and Czech crown, dealers said on Friday.
The rouble is not yet fully convertible, and within the restrictions of the present system has recently been strong.

But as the authorities open up the government securities market and proceed with rouble convertibility, the Russian currency will become increasingly susceptible to the pressures of the international market, they said.
"Previously our markets used to be virtually isolated, but now they've become part of the international market," said Aljba-Alliance chief dealer Dmitry Slobodnik.

"Since the new year, for example, MinFin bonds have started to react keenly to every change in U.S. economic indicators and have lost their national character...and later we will see that in rouble deposits," he said.
Central Bank Deputy Chairman Andrei Kozlov said the integration of Russia's markets with global markets was inexorable but this need not pose dangers for the rouble.
"The question is how much the Central Bank can stop external factors influencing the currency. So far we are coping, and we will continue to do so," Kozlov told Reuters.
"I hope that in 1998 the number of instruments in which non-residents can invest in Russia will be bigger," he added.
The central bank keeps the rouble within currency bands, known as a corridor, which allow it to depreciate gently at a predictable rate, as with a crawling peg.
The 1997 corridor will see the rouble in a 5,730-6,350 per dollar range at the end of December against 5,500-6,100 at the start of the year.

The Central Bank will probably announce in November whether it will continue the corridor, and if so on what terms. But Central Bank Chairman Sergei Dubinin said this week he did not expect any dramatic changes in currency policy in the near term.

The rouble, trading on Friday at about 5,770 per dollar, has never moved outside the corridor since the system was introduced in mid-1995, or even strayed outside the narrower bid/offer spread set every day within the corridor by the central bank.
On the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX) January 1998 $1,000 future contracts closed on Thursday at 5,987, well within the corridor for the end of 1997.
Within the corridor the rouble has been strong in recent weeks. The central bank's net international reserves rose to 11.3 trillion roubles on April 1 from 6.6 trillion on March 1.

Russian confidence in the rouble was reflected in its decision last June to sign up to Article Eight of the International Monetary Fund, requiring Russia to make the rouble convertible for current account, but not capital, transactions.

Central bank officials say Russia is unlikely to make the rouble fully convertible for capital transactions in the near future, because the authorities want to be able to regulate flows of hot money, which could destabilise not only the currency but also the government securities market.
Outside Russia's borders there is no developed rouble market, so that the rouble trades in a closed system.
That could change on January 1, 1998, when the final stage of liberalisation of the government securities market will allow foreign investors to repatriate profits from earnings at will.
At present profits can only be repatriated through forward and option deals at rates influenced by the central bank.
"The rouble doesn't attract non-residents in itself," said Bank Menatep dealer Mikhail Zaretsky.

"Their interest is concentrated in securities, and the rouble is a way in. It's difficult to speculate with the rouble because Western operators are not interested in speculating with the corridor," he said.
